title: The Escarpment of the Coral Triangle
premise: Orsen Zhou, a railroad engineer who keeps a private map of abandoned lines and keeps moving because staying means answering questions she can't afford, washes ashore in the Coral Triangle after a storm reveals a tide-cave that local legend says charges admission in memories. Inside she finds a drowned survey team's records pointing to a river whose source has been sealed by a mining consortium that owns the law in these islands. Pursued by the consortium's enforcer and sheltered by a ragtag crew of salvagers who slowly become the family she never let herself have, Orsen follows the river upstream to its forbidden source, where the mine's dam is about to fail and drown a village. She ends her running for good by blowing the evidence wide open, sacrificing her map, her anonymity, and nearly her life to give the river — and her found family — back their future.
about_author: Wendell Brightwater is the pen name of a former hydrographic surveyor who spent six years charting coastlines between Borneo and Sulawesi before turning to fiction. He writes adventure novels about people who find belonging in the last unmapped places on earth.

chapters.title: The Map of Closed Lines
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Aboard a coastal freighter, she catalogs defunct rail spurs in her worn notebook, establishing her rule: never stay longer than a job. When the captain asks where she's from, she lies smoothly, but the reader sees the loneliness beneath. Emotional beat: guarded competence masking exile.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gave Back
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A storm grounds the freighter on a reef island; walking the drained tidal flats at dawn, she finds a cave mouth the sea only opens twice a year. Inside: rusted survey equipment and a brass tube of charts stamped with a name she recognizes from her own map. Beat: wonder cracking open her caution.

chapters.title: Admission Charged in Memories
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, with interludes of the dead surveyor's journal. The cave's carvings recount a village that sold its river to save itself — and regretted it. Orsen realizes the charts show a route upstream to a source marked FORBIDDEN. Beat: the pull of a mystery that feels personally addressed to her.

chapters.title: The Salvagers of Pulau Karang
chapters.summary: Multi-POV introduction of the crew: gruff captain Mei-Lin, engineer twins Sef and Dara, and old diver Pak Uda. They fish Orsen out of trouble with consortium scouts and offer work, not charity. Beat: first friction and first unexpected warmth.

chapters.title: Terms of Passage
chapters.summary: Mei-Lin's POV. Negotiation aboard the salvage boat Kestrel: Orsen trades engineering skill for passage upriver, hiding how much she already knows. The crew tests her; she passes by fixing their failing winch overnight. Beat: transactional trust beginning to bend toward real trust.

chapters.title: The Consortium's Long Shadow
chapters.summary: Enforcer Ravel Voss's POV. He reviews the drowned survey team's file and flags Orsen as a loose end. Cold, methodical, he boards a gunboat south. Beat: the hunter enters the story; stakes become mortal.

chapters.title: Upstream Against the Current
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The Kestrel fights the river's rapids; Orsen and Sef bond over machinery while Dara needles her about her past. First ambush by hired river pirates — repelled with Orsen's improvised engineering. Beat: camaraderie forged under fire.

chapters.title: The Village That Sold Its River
chapters.summary: Pak Uda's POV. The crew reaches a riverside village where elders remember the cave legends and confirm the consortium dammed the source twenty years ago, buying silence with jobs and fear. A child gives Orsen a carved token — safe passage. Beat: grief for a community complicit in its own loss.

chapters.title: Charts in a Dead Man's Hand
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Decoding the drowned surveyor's annotations, she discovers he was murdered for finding that the dam is structurally doomed. Her own maps of closed lines turn out to mirror his — the same hand trained her mentor. Beat: the past she fled connects to this fight whether she likes it or not.

chapters.title: Voss Closes In
chapters.summary: Alternating Voss and Mei-Lin POVs. Voss burns a supply post ahead of them; Mei-Lin must choose between cargo and speed. Orsen offers to scout alone; Mei-Lin refuses to split the crew. Beat: the found family solidifies against external threat.

chapters.title: Night on the Oxbow
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. Anchored in a quiet bend, the crew shares stories around a fire; Orsen, cornered gently, admits why she runs — a bridge collapse she was blamed for that wasn't her fault. Beat: vulnerability; belonging stops being theoretical.

chapters.title: The Toll Bridge Trap
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. Voss seizes the last crossing; the crew must run the gauntlet under fire. Orsen rigs a diversion using the river itself, flooding the toll station. They escape but lose their fuel cache. Beat: victory with a cost; Voss now knows exactly who she is.

chapters.title: Portage Through the Green Hell
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Hauling the boat overland through jungle; exhaustion, leeches, and Dara's heatstroke force Orsen to lead for the first time. She finds an old rail bed — one of her closed lines — cutting days off the portage. Beat: her exile's skills become gifts to others.

chapters.title: The Source Forbidden
chapters.summary: Mei-Lin's POV. They reach the hidden valley behind the dam: a drowned village preserved underwater, the original home the elders sold. Orsen surveys the dam face and confirms collapse within days. Beat: awe curdling into urgency.

chapters.title: Evidence and Leverage
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The dead surveyor hid his full report in the valley; retrieving it means diving the flooded ruins with Pak Uda. They get the documents but trigger a consortium sensor net. Beat: hope and alarm in equal measure.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Weir
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. A village guide sells their position to Voss to protect his own family — justice outside the law cuts both ways. Voss takes Mei-Lin hostage and demands the report. Beat: the family tested by someone else's desperation.

chapters.title: The Price of the River
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Trade negotiation at the weir goes wrong; Voss plans to kill witnesses and let the dam fail quietly, blaming nature. Orsen stalls him by revealing she can prove the collapse was foreseeable — making him an accessory, not an agent. Beat: wit versus violence; the clock runs down.

chapters.title: When the Dam Breaks
chapters.summary: Climax, multi-POV. The dam begins to fail early. Orsen leads a desperate effort to breach it in a controlled direction, saving the downstream villages while Voss tries to stop her to bury the evidence. Pak Uda dies holding the spillway gate. Beat: sacrifice, chaos, courage.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Orsen and Mei-Lin POV. With the flood receded, the crew broadcasts the surveyor's report via the salvagers' radio network; consortium officers are arrested by an embarrassed national government, and Voss vanishes into the delta, unfinished business. Beat: imperfect justice, hard-won.

chapters.title: What Orsen Buried
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. She burns her map of closed lines — the symbol of her running — and sends the truth about the bridge collapse to the engineers' board that once condemned her. Beat: letting go of the identity built from flight.

chapters.title: A Line That Stays Open
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The crew rebuilds the village jetty; the elders ask Orsen to survey a new rail spur to bring trade back. For the first time she signs her name to a project without an exit plan. Beat: belonging chosen, not stumbled into.

chapters.title: The Escarpment at Dawn
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, closing frame echoing chapter one. Standing on the escarpment above the freed river, she watches morning light hit water that finally runs unbroken to the sea. The Kestrel sounds its horn below — family, waiting, not chasing. Beat: stillness earned; the journey ends where stopping no longer costs.
